summary: Presents a timing model for sources, destinations, and transit nodes in Deterministic Networking (DetNet), and a methodology to compute end-to-end latency and backlog bounds for various queuing methods. This supports bounded latency with zero congestion loss. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some machines need messages to arrive on time, every time. This gives the math for working out the longest wait a message will ever have along its route.

subtitle: Computing guaranteed delivery times for critical industrial and real-time systems.

tldr.problem: Some applications (industrial automation, connected vehicles, smart grids) require guarantees that packets will arrive within a specific time, not just eventually. Standard networks cannot provide this guarantee because they are designed for best-effort delivery.
tldr.mechanism: DetNet (Deterministic Networking) provides a timing model and methodology to compute end-to-end latency bounds and calculate buffer sizes needed to guarantee zero congestion loss, using specific queuing mechanisms and admission control.
tldr.outcome: Engineers can now calculate, before deployment, exactly what maximum latency any packet will experience and size buffers accordingly, enabling critical applications to run on shared networks with guaranteed performance.

today: RFC 9320 is an Informational document published in November 2022 that provides the timing model and methodology for implementing deterministic networking. It is actively used by equipment manufacturers and network operators deploying DetNet solutions.

sections.title: Guaranteeing Delivery Times in Networks
sections.content:
This RFC provides a method for calculating latency bounds in Deterministic Networking (DetNet), a service that provides bounded latency and zero congestion loss. DetNet is designed for applications that must know, in advance, the worst-case time a packet will take to traverse a network.

DetNet flows are characterized by a maximum bandwidth (guaranteed by the sender or by metering) and a requirement for a guaranteed worst-case end-to-end latency. Before transmission, it is possible to calculate end-to-end latency bounds and the buffer space required at each node. The key insight is that if bandwidth is controlled and paths are fixed, latency becomes predictable rather than probabilistic.

DetNet is important for industrial automation (factories), connected vehicles, time-critical grid control, remote surgery, and other applications where a missed deadline is not just inconvenient but dangerous or financially devastating. This RFC presents the timing model and methodology used by management systems, control planes, and resource reservation algorithms to make these guarantees possible.
sections.eli5: Factories and cars need to know messages will arrive in time, every time. This explains the math to calculate exactly how long a message takes through the network.

sections.title: The DetNet Timing Model
sections.content:
DetNet models the delay experienced by a packet as it passes through each node in six components: output delay (selection to transmission), link delay (transmission time across the link), frame preemption delay (if interrupted), processing delay (reception to queue insertion), regulation delay (shaping), and queuing delay (waiting in queue).

These six delays vary at each hop. The critical insight is that variations in some delays (output and processing) require extra buffer space in the next hop to absorb them. The goal is to calculate an upper bound on each delay component, then sum them to get an end-to-end bound.

DetNet uses two approaches: static latency calculation knows all flows in advance and optimizes globally; dynamic latency calculation allows flows to be added or deleted while guaranteeing existing flows remain within their latency bounds. Dynamic calculation is simpler but yields less efficient use of network resources.
sections.eli5: Each hop in the network causes delay in six ways: getting out, traveling the link, being interrupted, being processed, being shaped, and waiting in queue. You add them up to find the total worst-case time.

sections.title: Computing End-to-End Latency and Buffer Requirements
sections.content:
End-to-end delay is split into non-queuing delay (sum of output, link, frame preemption, and processing delays at all hops) and queuing delay (delays in regulators and queues). For certain queuing mechanisms, the end-to-end latency bound is less than the sum of per-hop bounds due to interactions between flows.

Buffer sizing is critical: too small and packets are dropped (congestion loss); too large and you waste memory and power. The buffer must hold packets in transmission plus packets waiting in queue. The formula accounts for the maximum number of input ports, maximum packet size, and the maximum delay experienced by any packet in the queuing subsystem.

A key issue is burstiness cascade: as a packet travels through the network, it collects jitter (timing variation) from earlier hops, which increases its burstiness, which increases jitter at the next hop. To handle this, regulators can reshape flows at each hop, but this is computationally expensive. An alternative is the interleaved regulator, which reshapes flows without per-flow queuing.
sections.eli5: The network causes timing variations that build up as packets travel. To prevent running out of buffer space, you must account for the worst-case accumulation of jitter. Reshaping at each hop helps but costs processing power.

sections.title: Queuing Mechanisms for Deterministic Networks
sections.content:
DetNet specifies several queuing mechanisms that ensure bounded latency. Frame preemption allows high-priority (express) frames to interrupt the transmission of lower-priority frames, reducing latency for critical traffic at the cost of preempted frames. Time-aware shaper uses time-synchronized gates that open and close on a schedule, controlling which queues can transmit at which times, similar to a traffic light.

Credit-based shaper (CBS) assigns a credit to each traffic class based on its guaranteed rate and decreases credit as traffic is sent. A class can only transmit when it has positive credit. This ensures no class can monopolize the link while still allowing different classes different service levels.

Cyclic Queuing and Forwarding (CQF) divides time into fixed cycles and assigns each DetNet flow to specific slots within each cycle, much like a train schedule. Guaranteed Service provides each flow a dedicated rate and latency through each node.

Each mechanism has trade-offs: some are simple to implement but provide loose bounds, others provide tight bounds but require clock synchronization or complex scheduling. The choice depends on the application and network constraints.
sections.eli5: Different methods control which messages get sent when. Some use priority interrupts, some use time schedules, some use credit systems, some use fixed time slots like a train schedule.

sections.title: Achieving Zero Congestion Loss
sections.content:
A core DetNet property is zero congestion loss — packets are never dropped due to queue overflow because resources are reserved in advance. To achieve this, the network must be sized such that buffers never overflow even in the worst case.

The paradox of DetNet is that it uses significant bandwidth to guarantee latency. Instead of statistical multiplexing (where you assume not all users will be active at once), DetNet reserves capacity for the worst case. This ensures latency but uses more network resources than best-effort systems.

Buffer requirements are computed during admission control: when a new DetNet flow is requested, the network checks whether buffers at each hop can absorb the new flow without exceeding capacity. If yes, the flow is admitted and parameters are configured. If no, the flow is rejected or rerouted.

The DocNet model accounts for the possibility of packet reordering within a node and provides bounds on these reorderings, ensuring that regulators can still function correctly even when packets arrive out of order internally.
sections.eli5: Nothing gets dropped because the network is sized to handle everything. You pay for this safety with extra bandwidth reserved just in case.
